task_prompts.packaging-9c652e4b: `Pylock.select()` always prefers a wheel over a source distribution when both are available and the wheel is compatible, with no way to override that for specific packages. Please add a way to pass a predicate (taking the normalized package name and returning a bool) to `select()` that lets a caller indicate that the source distribution should be preferred over an otherwise-compatible wheel for a given package. When the predicate returns true for a package that has both a compatible wheel and an sdist, `select()` should choose the sdist; when it's false, or when only a wheel is available, the existing wheel-preferring behavior should be unchanged. It should also work correctly when no sdist exists at all (the predicate may still be called, but selection should fall back to the wheel).
task_prompts.packaging-fe18f139:
When a `Requirement` string contains an arbitrary-equality specifier list where one of the comma-separated values is itself invalid, the resulting error message is confusing/unhelpful instead of clearly pointing at the bad specifier. For example:

```python
from packaging.requirements import Requirement
Requirement("demo===x,y")
```

This should raise `InvalidRequirement` with a message like `"Invalid specifier: 'y'"`, but currently the underlying specifier error isn't surfaced clearly through `Requirement`. This also affects `Requirement.__setstate__` when restoring from a string that has this kind of invalid specifier — it should raise `TypeError` with a message indicating the requirement can't be restored, same as for any other invalid requirement string. Please fix requirement parsing/unpickling so invalid specifier errors are reported clearly and consistently.
task_prompts.packaging-189a76d5:
Marker and Requirement parsing silently accepts trailing garbage at the end of the string instead of treating it as a syntax error, as long as it's a line break. For example:

```python
from packaging.markers import Marker
Marker('python_version >= "3"\n')
```

This should raise `InvalidMarker` (a trailing `\n`, `\r`, or `\r\n` is not valid syntax), and the same applies to `Requirement` strings like `"name>=1\n"` or `'name; python_version >= "3"\r\n'`, which should raise `InvalidRequirement`. Meanwhile, trailing horizontal whitespace (plain spaces or tabs) at the end of a marker or requirement string should continue to be accepted and ignored, e.g. `Marker('python_version >= "3" ')` should still equal `Marker('python_version >= "3"')`. Please fix the parser so it correctly requires true end of input and rejects trailing line breaks while still tolerating trailing horizontal whitespace.
task_prompts.packaging-826426fc: When calling `Pylock.select()` with an explicitly empty `tags` list (`tags=[]`), it seems to be treated the same as "no tag filter" instead of "no wheel tags are acceptable". For example, building a Pylock that contains both a wheel and an sdist for a package and calling `pylock.select(tags=[], environment=...)` currently returns the host-compatible wheel, but since an empty tag sequence should mean no wheel can match, it should instead fall back to the sdist, and if only a wheel is available (no sdist) it should raise a `PylockSelectError` saying no wheel matched and no sdist is available. Please fix `select()` to respect an explicitly empty tag sequence rather than treating it as unset.
task_prompts.packaging-26fa1d42: `packaging.tags.parse_tag()` (and by extension wheel filename parsing) accepts interpreter components that are not valid identifiers, letting malformed values through. For example, `tags.parse_tag("2.7.6-none-any")` or parsing a wheel filename like `playlyfe-0.1.1-2.7.6-none-any.whl` succeeds and expands into tags with a numeric-looking interpreter instead of being rejected, while things like `py3.2-none-any` or `py+3-none-any` also slip through. Valid interpreter tags should be identifiers (e.g. `cp311`, `sillywalk`, `_custom`), so anything else should raise `InvalidTag` with a message indicating an invalid interpreter. Please add proper validation for the interpreter component of a tag.
task_prompts.packaging-2d873eb6:
When writing RFC822 metadata headers via `Metadata.as_rfc822()`, only `\n` line boundaries in header values get folded/escaped; other line-boundary characters such as `\r`, `\v`, `\f`, `\x1c`-`\x1e`, `\x85`, `\u2028`, and `\u2029` are passed through unfolded. Depending on the Python version this either lets a value like `"Hello\rWorld"` inject what looks like an extra header line into the generated metadata, or causes `email` to raise `HeaderWriteError` when writing it. For example:
```python
from packaging.metadata import Metadata
meta = Metadata.from_raw({"version": "1.2.3", "name": "packaging", "author": "Hello\rWorld", "metadata_version": "2.3"})
meta.as_rfc822().as_string()
```
All of these line-boundary characters should be folded consistently like `\n` is, and similarly `Summary` validation should reject values containing any of them, not just `\n`. Please fix this.
task_prompts.packaging-b80e6eb0:
`Pylock.select()` doesn't correctly handle an explicitly empty `environments` list. If `environments=[]` is set on a `Pylock` (as opposed to `environments=None`, meaning no restriction was declared), calling `select()` should behave as if no environment in the lock is compatible with the current one — i.e. it should raise the same "no matching environment" error as when a real marker fails to match — but instead it currently doesn't. Reproduction:
```python
pylock = Pylock(lock_version=Version("1.0"), created_by="some_tool", environments=[], packages=[])
list(pylock.select(tags=..., environment=...))
```
This should raise the same error as passing `environments=[Marker('python_version == "3.14"')]` against a non-matching environment, while `environments=None` should still mean no filtering is applied. Please fix `select()` to distinguish these cases correctly.
task_prompts.packaging-4e79787a:
`packaging.tags.cpython_tags()`, `generic_tags()`, and `compatible_tags()` don't respect an explicitly empty `platforms` argument. Passing `platforms=[]` should mean no platform tags apply and the wheel/pure-python-platform-specific tags should be skipped, but currently it seems to fall back to auto-detecting the platform instead of yielding nothing for that part. For example:
```python
from packaging import tags
list(tags.cpython_tags((3, 11), abis=["whatever"], platforms=[]))  # should be []
list(tags.generic_tags("sillywalk", ["abi"], []))  # should be []
```
Please fix these functions to treat an explicitly empty platforms iterable as "no platform-specific tags" rather than "use the default platform".
task_prompts.packaging-f14a0933: The `~=` (compatible release) operator in `Specifier` can incorrectly accept invalid version strings due to unscoped case-insensitive matching of the pre/post-release words in the regex, similar to a previously fixed issue with the `==` operator's local version suffix. For example, `Specifier("~=1.2.3prev\u0131ew1")` and `Specifier("~=1.2.3po\u017ft1")` (using Turkish dotless-i and long-s, which fold to ASCII letters under Unicode case-insensitive matching) are currently accepted as valid specifiers when they should raise `InvalidSpecifier`. Please scope the relevant regex groups so this Unicode case-folding no longer causes invalid specifiers to be accepted for `~=`.
task_prompts.packaging-55cbf1b9: In `packaging._ranges`, unbounded lower/upper bounds don't consistently compare or hash as equal depending on how they were constructed, which lets them sort inconsistently relative to each other. For instance, `LowerBound(None, True)` and `LowerBound(None, False)` both represent "negative infinity" and should be treated as the exact same value (equal to `NEG_INF`, same hash, ordering comparisons all treating them as equal), but currently `LowerBound(None, True).inclusive` doesn't normalize and equality/hash/ordering between these two spellings is inconsistent — the same problem applies to `UpperBound`/`POS_INF`. This can cause version ranges with unbounded ends to sort or deduplicate incorrectly. Please fix bound handling so unbounded lower and upper bounds each have a single canonical representation for equality, hashing, and ordering.
